E1.title: Module 1 — hybrid segmentation versus each component alone
notes: Conversion is an evaluation column only — never a clustering feature and never a rule input — so the separation is not circular.
Segments under 30 users are reported but excluded from the separation statistic.

The hybrid separates conversion no better than the rules alone (0.3838 against 0.3837). On this metric the clustering adds nothing, and the honest reading is that the rules carry the commercial signal. The hybrid earns its place elsewhere — it produces a calibrated confidence from the level of agreement between three independent methods, and it is the vote that makes cold start explicit — but not by separating conversion further.

Clustering alone barely separates conversion at all. It groups users by behavioural similarity, which is not the same thing as grouping them by commercial value — and this is the measurement that shows the difference rather than assuming it.
Silhouette is 0.087: the clusters overlap heavily in feature space. The segments are commercially useful without being geometrically clean, and reporting only the separation would hide that.

E2.title: Module 1 — leakage and the deleted cold-start segment
notes: Leakage barely moves accuracy (0.9213 against 0.9200) but inflates certainty by a factor of 150: 450 users come out at confidence 1.00 with the rule label among the inputs, against 3 without it. Accuracy is not what the defect corrupts — the confidence attached to every downstream decision is.
That is also why it survived review. Nothing fails, no test goes red, and the only symptom is a confidence column that looks impressive.

Even the corrected accuracy should not be quoted as generalisation to a new audience. The rule component of the target is a deterministic function of these same features, so this measures internal consistency; the engine reports that caveat in its own diagnostics.
Under the notebook's vote order the cold-start segment loses 36 of 163 users on this dataset. On the live audience it went to zero — a contribution deleted by its own pipeline.

E3.title: Module 2 — fixed vs trigger vs hybrid, over 30 paired seeds
notes: Every seed puts the same 8,000 users through all three policies, so the comparison is paired and the tests are paired accordingly.
Conversions per 1,000 sends is the metric to read. User-level conversion rate rises with message volume, which would hand the win to `fixed` for sending more rather than for sending better.

Simulated response. Module 2's simulator draws each user's behaviour from segment-level propensities calibrated against the dataset's own conversion rates; the policies are real code, the reactions are not observed behaviour.
trigger leads fixed by 3.3 conversions per 1,000 sends for 3 extra decision rules — the trade the report has to argue.

Messages per user differ sharply (fixed 4.00, trigger 1.32, hybrid 3.05). A policy that stops early is rewarded by a per-send metric and penalised by a per-user one; both are reported so the choice of metric is visible rather than decisive.

E4.title: Module 3 — attribution model comparison and disagreement
notes: first_touch has the lowest error, but its interval overlaps linear's — with only 5 channels to average over, the ranking is suggestive rather than established.
20% of converting journeys had a single touchpoint (mean 1.8 distinct channels). On those, every model agrees by arithmetic — the agreement is not evidence.
first_touch and last_touch disagree over 68% of all attributed credit on the same journeys — the single clearest argument in this project against trusting one attribution model.

Ground-truth scoring is only possible on simulated journeys, where the true channel influence is known by construction. No such column exists for a real audience, which is why the live half reports disagreement rather than accuracy.

E5.title: Module 3 — prediction quality, and its transfer to another audience
notes: conversion: xgboost (AUC 0.973) clears the baseline with no interval overlap.
drop_off: xgboost (AUC 0.990) clears the baseline with no interval overlap.

These models are fitted on Module 3's simulator. Applying them to the imported audience is a transfer across distributions: the ranking is usable, the absolute probabilities are not calibrated for it.

E6.title: Module 4 — goal and tone classification, TF-IDF versus Sentence-BERT

e6_mcnemar.note: each model is right where the other is wrong exactly 8 times — the disagreements cancel entirely
A is right where B is wrong more often than the reverse

notes: `campaign_goal`: the two approaches are statistically indistinguishable on this corpus (McNemar p=1.000, 16 disagreements). Choosing TF-IDF is then a decision about cost and interpretability, not about accuracy — which is a stronger argument than claiming it is more accurate.
`tone`: humorous has fewer than 2 examples — cannot be split, cannot be learned, and cannot be evaluated. Reported, not hidden.

`tone`: the two approaches are statistically indistinguishable on this corpus (McNemar p=0.727, 8 disagreements). Choosing TF-IDF is then a decision about cost and interpretability, not about accuracy — which is a stronger argument than claiming it is more accurate.
`tone`: best macro-F1 0.732 (tfidf + logistic) against a majority baseline of 0.112; accuracy 0.818 against 0.386. The accuracy gap flatters the model far more than the macro-F1 gap does.
`campaign_goal`: best macro-F1 0.500 (tfidf + logistic) against a majority baseline of 0.148; accuracy 0.772 against 0.588. The accuracy gap flatters the model far more than the macro-F1 gap does.

E7.title: Module 4 — engagement prediction, leakage and the absence of signal
notes: The leaky model scores far better on every metric. That is the point: nothing about the training run flags the defect, and the corrected number looks like a regression to anyone reading only the headline.
Spearman is the metric to read. The model ranks candidate captions; it is not required to predict an engagement rate in absolute terms.

None of the 8 text features correlates with engagement after Holm–Bonferroni correction. This is a property of the dataset, not a modelling failure — no model can extract a signal that is not there, and the honest response is to reduce the weight this score carries in content ranking rather than to keep tuning.
The corrected model's rank correlation is 0.012 [-0.028, 0.054] — the interval spans zero, so no ranking skill is demonstrated on held-out data.
